parole.significato: to bear, to give birth to
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch baren. The a in the stem and the weak inflection are unetymological, but their origin is unknown. The form developed from and displaced the older strong beren (still found in modern ontberen), from Old Dutch beran, from Proto-Germanic *beraną. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *b

parole.significato: to thunder, to make a thunderous sound
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bulderen, also boldren, from Old Dutch *bulron, further etymology unknown. Possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to make a loud sound”) via Middle Low German bulderen.

From Middle Dutch dertel, derten; further etymology unclear. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰerh₃- (“to leap, spring forth”); if so, Germanic relatives would include Danish dirre (“to tremble, quiver”) and Swedish darra.

From Middle Dutch huken, possibly by metathesis from a form *huck(e)ren, frequentative of hucken (“to crouch”). Of obscure ultimate origin, but perhaps from the root of words like hoog (“high”), heup (“hip”), heuvel (“hill”), or ultimately related to Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to bend, curve”), sim
Compare German knabbern (“to nibble”). Both could ultimately be from Proto-Indo-European *gnet- (“to press”), or imitative.

parole.significato: calf, fleshy part of the lower leg
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch cute (“spawn; fleshy body part, e.g. buttock, calf, back of the upper arm”). Further origin unknown. Possibly related with kont (“buttocks”) or with Sanskrit गुद (guda, “entrails”); according to Pokorny, all are derived Proto-Indo-European *gēu- (“to arch bend”), see also German Ku

From Middle Dutch lollen. May ultimately derive from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂- (an expressive root and presumably an onomatopoeia). If so, then cognate with Latin lāmentum, Ancient Greek λῆρος (lêros), λάλος (lálos), λάσκω (láskō). Due to the association with lul (“cock”), the word may today be reg
From Middle Dutch rōve. Cognate with Old High German ruf (Luxembourgish Roff), Old Norse hrufa (English dandruff). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *krewp-.
From Middle Dutch rûun. Cognate with Middle Low German rûne, Middle High German rūn. Further origin unknown; possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(H)rewH- (“to dig out, rip off”).

parole.significato: a set of twenty, a score (usually said of eggs)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stîge. Has been compared to Ancient Greek στίχος (stíkhos, “row, line”). If indeed related, from Proto-Indo-European *steygʰ- (“to walk, go, ascend”). Cognate with Middle Low German stîge (whence German Stiege), Crimean Gothic stega (“twenty”).

parole.significato: the end of a rope or chain
parole.testo: Probably from Proto-Indo-European *dewmbʰ- (“penis, tail, rod”), and cognate with German Zumpf (“penis”), Persian دنب (donb, “tail”), and perhaps Proto-Germanic *tuppaz (“top”).
